description: How commodities behave when cooked: functional properties, dry and moist heat methods.
content_html:
Why Commodities Behave Differently in the Kitchen

Pick up a raw egg and a hard-boiled one — they feel and behave completely differently, yet the only thing that changed was heat. This is the heart of food science: every commodity has working characteristics that determine what happens when you cook with it. Understanding these characteristics explains why a sponge cake rises, why a sauce thickens, why a stir-fry browns — and crucially, why things can go wrong.

Key Fact

The spec lists ten functional / chemical properties across four ingredient categories. Learn them in groups: carbohydrates (gelatinisation, dextrinization); fats (shortening, aeration, plasticity, emulsification); proteins (coagulation, foam formation, gluten formation, denaturation); fruit and vegetables (enzymic browning, oxidisation).

Carbohydrates: Gelatinisation and Dextrinization

Gelatinisation is what turns a thin liquid into a thick sauce. When a roux-based béchamel sauce is heated on the hob, the starch granules in the flour absorb water, swell and eventually burst, releasing amylose chains that tangle together and thicken the sauce. The process is essentially complete above 80 °C. If the sauce is not stirred during this stage, clumps of gelatinised starch form — the lumpy white sauce so familiar from school kitchens. Stirring distributes the heat evenly and keeps the granules from aggregating.

Dextrinization happens when starch is dry-heated. Toast the surface of a slice of bread under the grill and you will see dextrinization at work: the starch molecules on the surface break down into shorter chains (dextrins), producing the golden-brown colour and slightly crisp texture of toast. This is a different reaction from gelatinisation, which requires water. Dextrinization also contributes to the crust of a baked loaf and the croutons in a salad.

Fats: Shortening, Aeration, Plasticity and Emulsification

Fats are among the most functionally versatile commodities. Shortening describes the way fat coats flour particles and prevents gluten strands from forming long networks — this is exactly what you want in shortcrust pastry, where the goal is a crumbly, tender texture rather than chew. Aeration occurs when fat (butter or margarine) is creamed vigorously with sugar: the mechanical action forces air into the fat, creating tiny bubbles that expand in the oven and contribute to a light sponge. Plasticity refers to the ability of solid fats to be spread, rolled or moulded at room temperature — important for laminated pastries such as croissants, where butter must be rolled into layers without melting. Emulsification is the ability to hold oil and water together. Egg yolk contains lecithin, a natural emulsifier, which is why adding egg yolk to a vinaigrette produces a temporarily stable suspension, and why hollandaise sauce can hold butter in a water-based liquid without separating.

Proteins: Coagulation, Foam Formation, Gluten Formation and Denaturation

Coagulation is the reason scrambled eggs solidify when heated: liquid egg protein denatures and then bonds together, forming a solid curd. In a quiche filling, the protein in the egg-and-milk mixture sets in the oven, encasing the other ingredients. A related property is foam formation: whisking egg whites stretches and denatures the protein, which wraps around tiny air bubbles and stabilises them — giving a meringue mixture its volume. The foam collapses if fat is accidentally introduced (a trace of egg yolk, a greasy bowl), because fat destroys the protein film around the air bubbles.

Gluten formation occurs in wheat-flour doughs. Glutenin and gliadin proteins in flour absorb water and, when the dough is kneaded, align and bond into a continuous elastic network. This network traps carbon dioxide produced by yeast fermentation, causing the dough to rise. Over-working a pastry dough activates the same protein network, producing a tough, chewy result instead of a short, crumbly one — which is why pastry-making guides say “handle the dough as little as possible.”

Students often use these terms interchangeably — but they describe different stages. Denaturation is the unfolding of the protein molecule’s three-dimensional shape. It can be caused by heat (frying an egg), acid (marinating chicken in lemon juice tightens the flesh), or physical action (whisking egg whites). Coagulation is the next stage: the denatured (unfolded) proteins bond together, forming a solid structure. Both processes are irreversible. In an exam question about why scrambled egg solidifies, the full answer is: “The proteins in the egg denature as they are heated (because heat breaks the bonds holding the protein in its three-dimensional shape); the denatured proteins then coagulate, bonding together to form a solid curd.”

Fruit and Vegetables: Enzymic Browning and Oxidisation

Enzymic browning is why a freshly sliced apple turns brown within minutes of being cut. The cut surface exposes phenolic compounds to polyphenol oxidase enzymes; these react with oxygen from the air to produce brown melanin pigments. In cooking, enzymic browning can be prevented by: covering the cut surface with acidulated water (vitamin C from lemon juice lowers pH, inhibiting the enzyme); blanching (brief boiling denatures the enzyme); or vacuum packing (removing oxygen). In the production of black tea, enzymic browning is deliberately encouraged to develop colour and flavour. Oxidisation is the broader term for nutrient loss (particularly vitamin C) when fruit and vegetables are cut, stored or cooked — oxygen in the air, heat and water all accelerate the process.

Dry vs Moist Methods of Cooking

The cooking method determines which of a commodity’s working characteristics are activated. Dry methods include roasting, baking, grilling, frying and dry-frying. In dry methods, surface moisture evaporates quickly, temperatures at the surface can reach well above 100 °C, and reactions like dextrinization, the Maillard reaction, and fat rendering take place. A Sunday roast chicken in the oven is a showcase for dry-heat cooking: the proteins denature and coagulate in the breast, fat renders from the skin, and the Maillard reaction creates the brown crust and rich flavour. Moist methods include boiling, steaming, poaching, braising and stewing. Water limits temperatures to 100 °C at atmospheric pressure; this prevents surface browning but can cause water-soluble vitamins (B vitamins, vitamin C) to leach into the cooking water. Steaming is preferable to boiling for retaining micronutrients in vegetables.

Key Fact

The Maillard reaction requires amino acids AND reducing sugars AND a temperature above approximately 140 °C. It produces brown colour and complex flavour. It is responsible for the crust of a loaf of bread, the colour of a grilled steak, and the golden skin of a roast potato. It is NOT the same as caramelisation, which involves only sugar.

A very common exam error is to confuse these two starch reactions. Remember: gelatinisation needs water (it thickens a sauce, a gravy, or a custard); dextrinization needs dry heat (it browns the surface of toast, bread crusts, and croutons). Both involve starch molecules changing structure, but they are triggered by completely different conditions. A quick mnemonic: “G for gravy (gelatinisation), D for dry-toasted (dextrinization).”
exam_tip_html: On 6-mark Explain (Extended Response) questions about working characteristics, the most common error is naming a functional property without applying it to a specific dish. The command word ‘Explain’ requires you to give reasons and causes. Compare these two answers: Weak: “Aeration is when fat traps air.” Strong: “Aeration occurs when butter is creamed with sugar — the mechanical action forces air bubbles into the fat, and because these bubbles expand during baking, the Victoria sandwich develops a light, open crumb structure.” The second answer names the commodity, names the dish, explains the mechanism with a because-link, and describes the outcome. Each of those elements contributes marks. For any working characteristic question, follow this structure: name the property → name the ingredient → name the dish → explain the mechanism → describe the result.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The ten key working characteristics to know are: gelatinisation and dextrinization (carbohydrates); shortening, aeration, plasticity and emulsification (fats); coagulation, foam formation, gluten formation and denaturation (proteins); enzymic browning and oxidisation (fruit and vegetables).
  • Dry methods (roasting, baking, grilling) activate browning reactions (Maillard, dextrinization) because temperatures can exceed 100 °C; moist methods (boiling, steaming) limit temperature to 100 °C and can cause water-soluble vitamin loss.
  • Denaturation (unfolding of protein) and coagulation (bonding of unfolded proteins) are two distinct, sequential stages — using both terms correctly in an exam answer shows precise knowledge.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes gelatinisation?
A) Starch granules brown when heated without water above 160 degrees C
B) Starch granules absorb water, swell and burst when heated above approximately 60 degrees C, thickening a liquid
C) Protein chains unfold and bond together when heated, forming a solid
D) Sugar caramelises at high temperatures, producing a brown colour and sweet flavour
practice_questions.marks: B) Starch granules absorb water, swell and burst when heated above approximately 60 degrees C, thickening a liquid. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the two physical states of cooking classified as dry methods and moist methods.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for naming both dry heat methods AND moist heat methods. Acceptable answers for dry include: roasting, baking, grilling, frying, stir-frying. Acceptable answers for moist include: boiling, steaming, poaching, braising, stewing. [1 mark for clearly identifying both categories with at least one example each]

practice_questions.text: Give two reasons why steaming is preferable to boiling when cooking green vegetables.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per reason, up to 2 marks. Acceptable answers: steaming prevents water-soluble vitamins (e.g. vitamin C, B vitamins) from leaching into the cooking water (1); steaming retains the colour and texture of green vegetables better than boiling (1); in steaming, vegetables do not come into direct contact with the water, reducing nutrient loss (1). Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe three functional properties of fats and oils that are important in baking a Victoria sandwich.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per functional property that is named and described in context, up to 3 marks. Acceptable answers: aeration — butter is creamed with sugar to trap air bubbles, giving the cake a light texture (1); shortening — fat coats the flour particles and prevents long gluten networks forming, giving a tender crumb (1); plasticity — the fat is solid at room temperature but softens easily when creamed, making it workable (1). Do not award marks for simply naming a property without describing it.

practice_questions.text: Callum is making a wholemeal loaf. He kneads the dough for 10 minutes and leaves it to prove. Explain why kneading is an essential step in bread making.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per explanation (1 for the point, 1 for a linked reason using because/this means that/as a result), up to 4 marks. Kneading develops gluten: kneading aligns the glutenin and gliadin proteins in the flour and encourages them to bond into an elastic network, because mixing with water activates these proteins (2). The gluten network traps carbon dioxide: once the dough has a strong gluten structure, the gas produced by yeast fermentation is held within the dough, which means that the loaf rises to give a light, open crumb (2). Without adequate kneading, gluten development is poor and the loaf will be dense and heavy (bonus development point).

practice_questions.text: Explain why enzymic browning occurs when fruit and vegetables are cut, and describe three methods a cook can use to prevent it.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5-6 marks): Clear explanation of the enzymic mechanism (polyphenol oxidase + oxygen + phenolic compounds = brown melanin pigment), applied to a named food (apple, avocado, potato). Three prevention methods each described with a scientific reason (acid lowers pH and inhibits the enzyme; blanching denatures the enzyme by heat; vacuum packing removes oxygen). Accurate food-science vocabulary throughout. Secure (3-4 marks): Explanation of browning with partial mechanism (enzyme + oxygen = brown); two or three prevention methods identified, some with reasons. Developing (1-2 marks): Browning described without mechanism; prevention methods listed without explanation. Emerging (0 marks): No relevant content. Indicative content: cut fruit/vegetables expose phenolic compounds to the enzyme polyphenol oxidase and to oxygen in the air; the enzyme catalyses a reaction that produces brown melanin pigments; prevention: submerging in acidulated water (lemon juice or vinegar) lowers pH and inhibits the enzyme; blanching briefly denatures the enzyme with heat; vacuum packing removes oxygen so the reaction cannot occur; covering with cling film limits oxygen contact.

knowledge_checks.q: What is the correct term for starch granules absorbing water and swelling when heated above 60 degrees C?
Enzymic browning occurs when cut fruit is exposed to _____ in the air, activating the enzyme polyphenol oxidase.
Which of the following best describes the Maillard reaction?
options: Starch swelling in water above 60 degrees C
Protein unfolding when exposed to acid
Browning of amino acids and sugars above approximately 140 degrees C in dry heat

knowledge_checks.q: In bread making, _____ development gives dough its stretchy, elastic structure that traps carbon dioxide from yeast.
Match each functional property to the correct ingredient and context:
right: Butter creamed with sugar in a Victoria sandwich
Starch thickening a white sauce on the hob
Egg proteins setting solid when scrambled eggs are heated

flashcard_questions.a: Starch granules absorb water above ~60 degrees C, swell and burst, thickening the liquid.
Starch on a surface browns in dry heat above ~160 degrees C, forming dextrins with a golden colour and nutty flavour.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between gelatinisation and dextrinization?
flashcard_questions.a: Gelatinisation needs water (thickens sauces); dextrinization needs dry heat (browns toast crusts).

flashcard_questions.q: What is shortening as a fat functional property?
flashcard_questions.a: Fat coats flour particles, preventing long gluten networks and giving a crumbly, tender texture.

flashcard_questions.q: What is aeration as a fat functional property?
flashcard_questions.a: Fat traps air bubbles when creamed with sugar, expanding during baking to give a light sponge.
The ability of a substance such as lecithin in egg yolk to keep oil and water in a stable suspension.
The irreversible unfolding of a protein's three-dimensional structure caused by heat, acid or physical action.
Denatured protein chains bond together, forming a solid or semi-solid structure.
A network of glutenin and gliadin proteins formed when flour is mixed with water and kneaded.
Cut fruit/vegetables turn brown when polyphenol oxidase reacts with oxygen, producing melanin pigment.
A non-enzymic browning of amino acids and reducing sugars above ~140 degrees C, producing brown colour and complex flavour.

flashcard_questions.q: Why can moist cooking methods cause vitamin C loss in vegetables?
flashcard_questions.a: Vitamin C is water-soluble and leaches into the cooking water; heat also destroys it.

flashcard_questions.q: How can enzymic browning in cut apples be prevented?
flashcard_questions.a: Cover with acidulated water (lemon juice), blanch the apple, or vacuum pack to remove oxygen.

glossary_terms.definition: The way a food ingredient behaves when it is prepared, mixed, heated or otherwise processed, including physical and chemical changes it undergoes.
The process by which starch granules absorb water when heated above approximately 60 degrees C, swell and burst, causing a liquid to thicken.
The browning of starch on the surface of a food subjected to dry heat above approximately 160 degrees C, producing dextrins and a golden colour.
The ability of a substance such as lecithin to keep fat and water mixed together in a stable suspension.
The irreversible unfolding of a protein's three-dimensional structure caused by heat, acid or physical action.
The bonding together of denatured protein chains to form a solid or semi-solid structure.
The development of an elastic protein network in wheat flour dough, formed when glutenin and gliadin absorb water and are kneaded.
The brown discolouration of cut fruit and vegetables caused by the enzyme polyphenol oxidase reacting with oxygen from the air.
A non-enzymic browning reaction between amino acids and reducing sugars that occurs above approximately 140 degrees C, producing brown colour and complex flavour.

hero_image_caption: Kneading bread dough develops gluten — one of ten key working characteristics that explain how commodities behave when heated, mixed or prepared.
